claim: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) allows activation of muscle fibers in the absence of voluntary force generation.
source: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) allows activation of muscle fibers in the absence of voluntary force generation.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing a known property of NMES, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Endurance neuromuscular stimulation (eNMES) improved all outcome measures in zebrafish dmd mutants.
source: Only endurance neuromuscular stimulation (eNMES) improved all outcome measures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing improvements in multiple measured parameters.

claim: eNMES improves muscle and neuromuscular junction morphology, swimming, and survival in zebrafish dmd mutants.
source: We found that eNMES improves muscle and neuromuscular junction morphology, swimming, and survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from birefringence, phalloidin staining, NMJ analysis, DanioVision swimming assays, and survival tracking.

claim: Heme oxygenase is required for eNMES-mediated improvement in dmd mutants.
source: Heme oxygenase and integrin alpha7 are required for eNMES-mediated improvement.
evidence: This claim is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments showing that hmox1a is necessary for eNMES benefits.

claim: Integrin alpha7 is required for eNMES-mediated improvement in dmd mutants.
source: Heme oxygenase and integrin alpha7 are required for eNMES-mediated improvement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using itga7 mutants showing no improvement with eNMES treatment.

claim: Individuals with DMD harbor mutations in the gene encoding the protein dystrophin.
source: Individuals with DMD harbor mutations in the gene encoding the protein dystrophin (Hoffman et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoffman et al., 1987.

claim: Dystrophin provides a link between the actin cytoskeleton and the extracellular matrix.
source: Dystrophin provides a link between the actin cytoskeleton and the extracellular matrix (ECM) and serves as a scaffold for the assembly of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC) within the sarcolemma (muscle plasma membrane) (Bonilla et al., 1988; Ervasti and Campbell, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bonilla et al., 1988 and Ervasti and Campbell, 1991.

claim: Dystrophin serves as a scaffold for the assembly of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC) within the sarcolemma.
source: Dystrophin provides a link between the actin cytoskeleton and the extracellular matrix (ECM) and serves as a scaffold for the assembly of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC) within the sarcolemma (muscle plasma membrane) (Bonilla et al., 1988; Ervasti and Campbell, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bonilla et al., 1988 and Ervasti and Campbell, 1991.

claim: The progressive muscle wasting and weakness in DMD is thought to result at least in part because the lack of dystrophin and the disruption of the DGC mechanically weaken the sarcolemma.
source: The progressive muscle wasting and weakness in DMD is thought to result at least in part because the lack of dystrophin and the disruption of the DGC mechanically weaken the sarcolemma.
evidence: This represents established scientific understanding about DMD pathophysiology.

claim: Stress placed on a mechanically weakened sarcolemma causes microlesions to develop along the sarcolemma, increasing calcium entry, which results in muscle protein degradation and muscle fiber necrosis.
source: Stress placed on a mechanically weakened sarcolemma causes microlesions to develop along the sarcolemma, increasing calcium entry, which results in muscle protein degradation and muscle fiber necrosis (Alderton and Steinhardt, 2000; Gailly, 2002; Gillis, 1996; Ruegg et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing the mechanism of muscle damage in DMD.

claim: Studies on the effects of activity on the progression of muscle disease in humans tend to be small with heterogeneous populations and a clear answer has not yet been established.
source: However, studies tend to be small with heterogeneous populations and a clear answer has not yet been established (Alemdaroğlu et al., 2015; Bushby et al., 2010; Gianola et al., 2013; Hyzewicz et al., 2015; Jansen et al., 2013; Markert et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple review and research articles.

claim: A 1966 study concluded that a resistance exercise program is most effective at increasing strength if instituted early in DMD disease.
source: For example, one study conducted in 1966 concluded that a resistance exercise program is most effective at increasing strength if instituted early in the disease, and a study conducted in 1981 concluded that resistance exercise negatively affects walking (Scott et al., 1981; Vignos and Watkins, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vignos and Watkins, 1966.

claim: A 1981 study concluded that resistance exercise negatively affects walking in DMD patients.
source: For example, one study conducted in 1966 concluded that a resistance exercise program is most effective at increasing strength if instituted early in the disease, and a study conducted in 1981 concluded that resistance exercise negatively affects walking (Scott et al., 1981; Vignos and Watkins, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scott et al., 1981.

claim: Recent studies suggest that bicycle ergometers can positively affect the quality of life early in the DMD disease course.
source: More recent studies have not examined resistance training but do suggest that bicycle ergometers can positively affect the quality of life early in the disease course (Alemdaroğlu et al., 2015; Jansen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alemdaroğlu et al., 2015 and Jansen et al., 2013.

claim: Studies using the mdx mouse to study the impact of exercise on disease progression take different approaches leading to disparate results.
source: Unfortunately, studies using the mdx mouse to study the impact of exercise on disease progression also take different approaches – treadmill training, voluntary wheel running, swimming, rotarod training – beginning at 3–96 weeks, leading to disparate results.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the literature on mdx mouse exercise studies.

claim: Some mdx mouse exercise studies demonstrate improvements in twitch tension, decreased necrosis, antioxidant capacities, and oxidative enzyme activity.
source: Collectively, studies demonstrate either improvements in twitch tension, decreased necrosis, antioxidant capacities, and oxidative enzyme activity (Baltgalvis et al., 2012; Call et al., 2008; Hulmi et al., 2013); or reduced strength, increased edema and inflammation, increases in reactive oxygen species, and increases in lipid peroxidation (Burdi et al., 2009; Faist et al., 2001; Kobayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baltgalvis et al., 2012; Call et al., 2008; Hulmi et al., 2013.

claim: Some mdx mouse exercise studies show reduced strength, increased edema and inflammation, increases in reactive oxygen species, and increases in lipid peroxidation.
source: Collectively, studies demonstrate either improvements in twitch tension, decreased necrosis, antioxidant capacities, and oxidative enzyme activity (Baltgalvis et al., 2012; Call et al., 2008; Hulmi et al., 2013); or reduced strength, increased edema and inflammation, increases in reactive oxygen species, and increases in lipid peroxidation (Burdi et al., 2009; Faist et al., 2001; Kobayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burdi et al., 2009; Faist et al., 2001; Kobayashi et al., 2012.

claim: Skeletal muscle fibers are influenced by the activity pattern imposed upon them, whether the activity is from the innervating neuron or electrical stimulation.
source: Skeletal muscle fibers are influenced by the activity pattern imposed upon them, whether the activity is from the innervating neuron or electrical stimulation (Pette and Vrbová, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pette and Vrbová, 1985.

claim: Guillaume Benjamin Amand Duchenne, the French neurologist who described DMD in 1861, proposed that super-imposing electrical stimulation on dystrophin-deficient muscles could serve as a potential therapy.
source: Early researchers, including Guillaume Benjamin Amand Duchenne, the French neurologist who described DMD in 1861, proposed that super-imposing electrical stimulation on dystrophin-deficient muscles could serve as a potential therapy (Barnard et al., 1986; Duchenne, 1870; Reichmann et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barnard et al., 1986; Duchenne, 1870; Reichmann et al., 1981.

claim: NMES delivers a series of waveforms of electrical current that is characterized by its frequency, amplitude, and pulse width.
source: NMES delivers a series of waveforms of electrical current that is characterized by its frequency, amplitude, and pulse width (or pulse duration) (Sheffler and Chae, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sheffler and Chae, 2007.

claim: The three parameters of NMES (frequency, amplitude, and pulse width) dictate the strength of the muscle contraction and the amount of force that is generated.
source: These three parameters dictate the strength of the muscle contraction and the amount of force that is generated.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about how NMES parameters affect muscle contraction.

claim: The main advantage of NMES is its ability to activate fast- and slow-twitch muscle fibers, resulting in hypertrophy without high-effort voluntary force generation.
source: The main advantage of NMES is its ability to activate fast- and slow-twitch muscle fibers, resulting in hypertrophy without high-effort voluntary force generation (Gondin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gondin et al., 2011.

claim: Only a few studies have examined the impact of NMES on muscle strength and function in humans with DMD.
source: However, only a few studies have examined the impact of NMES on muscle strength and function in humans (Scott et al., 1990; Scott et al., 1986; Zupan, 1992; Zupan et al., 1993) and the mdx mouse model of DMD (Dangain and Vrbova, 1989; Luthert et al., 1980; Vrbová and Ward, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The only clear conclusion from NMES studies in DMD is that NMES does not appear to be detrimental.
source: The only clear conclusion from these studies is that NMES does not appear to be detrimental.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature on NMES in DMD.

claim: Many molecular, ultrastructural, and histological features are shared between zebrafish and human muscle, including components of the DGC, the excitation-contraction coupling machinery, and the contractile apparatus.
source: Many molecular, ultrastructural, and histological features are shared between zebrafish and human muscle, including components of the DGC, the excitation-contraction coupling machinery, and the contractile apparatus (Dou et al., 2008; Dowling et al., 2009; Guyon et al., 2003; Parsons et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies comparing zebrafish and human muscle.

claim: Zebrafish exhibit reproducible, quantitative motor behaviors beginning at 1 day post-fertilization (dpf).
source: Further, zebrafish exhibit reproducible, quantitative motor behaviors beginning at 1 day post-fertilization (dpf) (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998), providing simple and noninvasive measures of muscle function.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998.

claim: Dystrophin-deficient zebrafish (sapjeta222a/ta222a, referred to as dmd mutants) exhibit severe structural and functional deficits by 4 dpf.
source: Dystrophin-deficient zebrafish, known as sapjeta222a/ta222a, and referred here as dmd mutants, are the smallest vertebrate model of DMD. These dmd mutants exhibit severe structural and functional deficits by 4 dpf, and die prematurely between their second and third weeks (Bassett et al., 2003; Berger et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bassett et al., 2003 and Berger et al., 2010.

claim: Zebrafish dmd mutants die prematurely between their second and third weeks.
source: Dystrophin-deficient zebrafish, known as sapjeta222a/ta222a, and referred here as dmd mutants, are the smallest vertebrate model of DMD. These dmd mutants exhibit severe structural and functional deficits by 4 dpf, and die prematurely between their second and third weeks (Bassett et al., 2003; Berger et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bassett et al., 2003 and Berger et al., 2010.

claim: Four NMES paradigms were designed that varied in pulse frequency and voltage.
source: We designed four different NMES paradigms ranging from high-frequency/low-voltage pulse trains to lower-frequency/higher-voltage pulse trains (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description in the text and the parameters shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The four NMES paradigms were named endurance NMES (eNMES), hypertrophy NMES (hNMES), strength NMES (sNMES), and power NMES (pNMES).
source: In order to easily differentiate these paradigms from each other, and because they were conceptually based on strength training paradigms that vary in the number of repetitions and load, we named these paradigms endurance NMES (eNMES), hypertrophy NMES (hNMES), strength NMES (sNMES), and power NMES (pNMES).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the naming convention used in the study.

claim: eNMES with high-frequency/low-voltage pulse trains elicited a fast but subtle tail beat.
source: As would be expected, eNMES with high-frequency/low-voltage pulse trains elicited a fast but subtle tail beat.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from Video 1 showing the tail beat patterns.

claim: With pNMES, the tail beat infrequently but bent to a much greater degree.
source: Conversely, with pNMES, the tail beat infrequently but bent to a much greater degree (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from Video 1 showing the tail beat patterns.

claim: None of the NMES paradigms consistently caused a dramatic change in either birefringence or EBD infiltration immediately after one session.
source: None of the NMES paradigms consistently caused a dramatic change in either birefringence (not shown) or EBD infiltration (Figure 1K, n = 5 embryos imaged, subjected to NMES, and imaged).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantification shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The four NMES paradigms did not cause immediate dramatic damage to the sarcolemma.
source: These results indicated that the four NMES paradigms did not cause immediate dramatic damage to the sarcolemma.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EBD infiltration data.

claim: During the training period, zebrafish completed three sessions of NMES, each session lasting 1 min, on three consecutive days (2, 3, and 4 dpf).
source: During the training period, zebrafish completed three sessions of NMES, each session lasting 1 min, on three consecutive days (2, 3, and 4 dpf) at the same time each day.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: Following the three training days, zebrafish entered the recovery period (5, 6, 7, and 8 dpf).
source: Following these three training days, zebrafish entered the recovery period (5, 6, 7, and 8 dpf).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: WT larvae with all four NMES paradigms were unaffected.
source: WT larvae with all four NMES paradigms were unaffected (Figure 2B1, C1, D1, E1, and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by the birefringence images shown in Figure 2.

claim: pNMES resulted in a slight but significant increase in birefringence compared to controls in dmd mutants.
source: pNMES resulted in a slight but significant increase in birefringence compared to controls (n = 32 control, n = 36 pNMES; p=0.0462; two biological replicates) (Figure 2B6, note also green arrows in Figure 2B4, B5).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative birefringence data shown in Figure 2B6.

claim: eNMES increased regeneration between 5 and 8 dpf in dmd mutants.
source: eNMES also increased regeneration between 5 and 8 dpf (n = 66 control, n = 66 eNMES; p=0.0037; five biological replicates) (Figure 2E6, note green arrows in Figure 2E4, E5).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative birefringence data shown in Figure 2E6.

claim: dmd mutants that underwent sNMES exhibited significantly lower changes in mean gray values compared to control dmd mutants.
source: In contrast, dmd mutants that underwent sNMES exhibited significantly lower changes in mean gray values compared to control dmd mutants (n = 49 control, n = 47 sNMES; p=0.0302; two biological replicates) (Figure 2C6)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative birefringence data shown in Figure 2C6.

claim: hNMES trended towards lowering birefringence in dmd mutants.
source: while hNMES trended towards lowering birefringence (n = 38 control, n = 48 hNMES; p=0.1322; two biological replicates) (Figure 2D6).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative birefringence data shown in Figure 2D6.

claim: Different NMES paradigms have different effects on muscle structure in zebrafish larvae.
source: These data indicate that different NMES paradigms do have different effects on muscle structure in zebrafish larvae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the birefringence data comparing different NMES paradigms.

claim: Muscle fibers in WT zebrafish are highly organized and linear.
source: Muscle fibers in WT zebrafish are highly organized and linear (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Many fibers in dmd mutants are thinner, wavy, and disorganized.
source: In contrast, many fibers in dmd mutants are thinner, wavy, and disorganized (Figure 3B, red arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neither sNMES nor hNMES affected the frequency of muscle fiber degeneration in dmd mutants.
source: Neither sNMES nor hNMES affected the frequency of muscle fiber degeneration (Figure 3D2, E2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of fiber detachments shown in Figure 3D2 and E2.

claim: eNMES resulted in fewer fibers degenerating compared to control dmd mutants.
source: However, similar to the results observed with birefringence, eNMES (n = 22 control, n = 18 eNMES; p=0.0191; one biological replicate) and pNMES (n = 12 control, n = 20 pNMES; p=0.0033; one biological replicate) resulted in fewer fibers degenerating compared to control dmd mutants (Figure 3C2, F2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of fiber detachments shown in Figure 3C2 and F2.

claim: pNMES resulted in fewer fibers degenerating compared to control dmd mutants.
source: However, similar to the results observed with birefringence, eNMES (n = 22 control, n = 18 eNMES; p=0.0191; one biological replicate) and pNMES (n = 12 control, n = 20 pNMES; p=0.0033; one biological replicate) resulted in fewer fibers degenerating compared to control dmd mutants (Figure 3C2, F2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of fiber detachments shown in Figure 3C2 and F2.

claim: eNMES and pNMES improve muscle structure in dmd larvae.
source: Taken together, the above data indicate that eNMES and pNMES improve muscle structure in dmd larvae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the birefringence and phalloidin staining data.

claim: The NMJ is altered in DMD patients and animal models for DMD.
source: The NMJ is altered in DMD patients and animal models for DMD (Ng and Ljubicic, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ng and Ljubicic, 2020.

claim: NMJ morphology has not been investigated in the zebrafish model for dmd prior to this study.
source: To our knowledge, NMJ morphology has not been investigated in the zebrafish model for dmd.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the NMJ analysis in this study.

claim: There are fewer NMJs in dmd mutants compared to WT larvae.
source: Note that there are many spiderweb-like NMJs throughout the segments in WT larvae (Figure 4A). In contrast, there are fewer NMJs in dmd mutants (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ staining images shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: pNMES did not change the number or length of NMJ skeletons in dmd mutants.
source: pNMES did not change the number or length of skeletons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of NMJ skeletons shown in Figure 4C.

claim: sNMES increased the number of NMJ skeletons in dmd mutants.
source: sNMES increased the number of skeletons (Figure 4D) (n = 18 control, n = 20 sNMES; p=0.0395; one biological replicate).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of NMJ skeletons shown in Figure 4D.

claim: hNMES increased NMJ skeleton length in dmd mutants.
source: Both hNMES (Figure 4E) and eNMES (Figure 4F) did not increase the number of skeletons but increased skeleton length (n = 15 control, n = 23 hNMES, p=0.0036; n = 18 control, n = 15 eNMES, p=0.0278; one biological replicate).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of NMJ skeleton length shown in Figure 4E.

claim: eNMES increased NMJ skeleton length in dmd mutants.
source: Both hNMES (Figure 4E) and eNMES (Figure 4F) did not increase the number of skeletons but increased skeleton length (n = 15 control, n = 23 hNMES, p=0.0036; n = 18 control, n = 15 eNMES, p=0.0278; one biological replicate).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of NMJ skeleton length shown in Figure 4F.

claim: All NMES paradigms, other than pNMES, improved the number or length of NMJs compared to control dmd mutants.
source: Thus, all NMES paradigms, other than pNMES, improved the number or length of NMJs compared to control dmd mutants.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the NMJ skeleton analysis data.

claim: Only eNMES improves both muscle and NMJ structure in dmd mutants.
source: The data presented thus far indicate that only eNMES improves both muscle and NMJ structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined muscle and NMJ structure data.

claim: eNMES was the only NMES paradigm that resulted in both increased distance and increased mean velocity compared to control dmd larvae.
source: As predicted, eNMES was the only NMES paradigm that resulted in both increased distance (n = 7 control, n = 11 eNMES; p<0.0001; one biological replicate) and increased mean velocity (n = 7 control, n = 11 eNMES; p<0.0001; one biological replicate) compared to control dmd larvae (Figure 5A4, B4).
evidence: This claim is supported by DanioVision swimming data shown in Figure 5A4 and B4.

claim: pNMES negatively affected swimming activity in dmd mutants.
source: pNMES negatively affected swimming activity (for both total distance and mean velocity: n = 20 control, n = 19 pNMES; p<0.0001; one biological replicate) (Figure 5A1,B1) despite having improved muscle structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by DanioVision swimming data shown in Figure 5A1 and B1.

claim: sNMES significantly reduced total distance and mean velocity in dmd mutants.
source: sNMES also significantly reduced total distance (n = 26 control, n = 23 sNMES; p<0.0001; one biological replicate) and mean velocity (n = 26 control, n = 23 sNMES; p<0.0001; one biological replicate) (Figure 5A2, B2)
evidence: This claim is supported by DanioVision swimming data shown in Figure 5A2 and B2.

claim: hNMES did not affect total distance or mean velocity in dmd mutants.
source: while hNMES did not affect these two measures (n = 20 control, n = 25 hNMES; p=0.1353 for total distance; p=0.1951 for mean velocity; one biological replicate) (Figure 5A3, B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by DanioVision swimming data shown in Figure 5A3 and B3.

claim: Three sessions of eNMES slightly but significantly extended the median age of survival for dmd mutants compared to unstimulated dmd mutants.
source: Three sessions of eNMES (n = 32 control, n = 37 eNMES; p<0.0001; two biological replicates), sNMES (n = 63 control, n = 55 sNMES; p=0.0004; two biological replicates), and pNMES (n = 37 control, n = 32 pNMES; p=0.0414; one biological replicate) slightly but significantly extended the median age of survival for dmd mutants compared to unstimulated dmd mutants (Figure 6A, B and D); with eNMES having the largest beneficial effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Three sessions of sNMES slightly but significantly extended the median age of survival for dmd mutants compared to unstimulated dmd mutants.
source: Three sessions of eNMES (n = 32 control, n = 37 eNMES; p<0.0001; two biological replicates), sNMES (n = 63 control, n = 55 sNMES; p=0.0004; two biological replicates), and pNMES (n = 37 control, n = 32 pNMES; p=0.0414; one biological replicate) slightly but significantly extended the median age of survival for dmd mutants compared to unstimulated dmd mutants (Figure 6A, B and D); with eNMES having the largest beneficial effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Three sessions of pNMES slightly but significantly extended the median age of survival for dmd mutants compared to unstimulated dmd mutants.
source: Three sessions of eNMES (n = 32 control, n = 37 eNMES; p<0.0001; two biological replicates), sNMES (n = 63 control, n = 55 sNMES; p=0.0004; two biological replicates), and pNMES (n = 37 control, n = 32 pNMES; p=0.0414; one biological replicate) slightly but significantly extended the median age of survival for dmd mutants compared to unstimulated dmd mutants (Figure 6A, B and D); with eNMES having the largest beneficial effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6.

claim: eNMES had the largest beneficial effect on survival among the NMES paradigms.
source: Three sessions of eNMES (n = 32 control, n = 37 eNMES; p<0.0001; two biological replicates), sNMES (n = 63 control, n = 55 sNMES; p=0.0004; two biological replicates), and pNMES (n = 37 control, n = 32 pNMES; p=0.0414; one biological replicate) slightly but significantly extended the median age of survival for dmd mutants compared to unstimulated dmd mutants (Figure 6A, B and D); with eNMES having the largest beneficial effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Three sessions of hNMES did not affect median survival age in dmd mutants.
source: Three sessions of hNMES, however, did not affect median survival age (n = 37 control, n = 32 hNMES; p=0.6788; one biological replicate) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Different NMES paradigms elicit different neuromuscular responses.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that different NMES paradigms elicit different neuromuscular responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on muscle structure, NMJ structure, swimming, and survival.

claim: Only eNMES improves neuromuscular structure, swimming, and life span.
source: Out of the four NMES paradigms we tested, only eNMES improves neuromuscular structure, swimming, and life span (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion shown in Figure 6E.

claim: eNMES significantly reduced muscle fiber detachments in dmd mutants.
source: We found that eNMES significantly reduced muscle fiber detachments in dmd mutants (n = 22 control, n = 18 eNMES; p=0.0191; one biological replicate) (Figure 3F2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of fiber detachments shown in Figure 3F2.

claim: dmd mutants completing three sessions of eNMES trend towards having higher percentages of healthy muscle compared to control dmd mutants.
source: From this analysis, we observed that dmd mutants completing three sessions of eNMES trend towards having higher percentages of health muscle compared to control dmd mutants (n = 17 control, n = 15 eNMES; p=0.2052; one biological replicate) (Figure 7A4).
evidence: This claim is supported by machine learning analysis of muscle health shown in Figure 7A4.

claim: Sarcomere length impacts muscle function.
source: Sarcomere length impacts muscle function (Moo and Herzog, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moo and Herzog, 2018.

claim: The amount of force generated by sarcomeres is dependent upon the amount of overlap between actin and myosin filaments.
source: Sarcomeres produce force through the cross-bridges formed between actin and myosin, and the amount of force generated is dependent upon the amount of overlap between these thick and thin filaments (Gordon et al., 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gordon et al., 1966.

claim: WT siblings exhibited a mean sarcomere length of 1.853 ± 0.1071 µm.
source: WT siblings exhibited a mean sarcomere length of 1.853 ± 0.1071 µm (Figure 7B1, B4).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy measurements shown in Figure 7B1 and B4.

claim: The mean sarcomere length in WT zebrafish at 8 dpf corresponds with sarcomere lengths previously published in 3 dpf WT zebrafish (1.86 ± 0.15 µm).
source: This result corresponded with sarcomere lengths previously published in 3 dpf WT zebrafish (1.86 ± 0.15 µm; Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2011.

claim: Sarcomeres were significantly shorter in dmd larvae with a mean length of 1.575 ± 0.1567 µm.
source: Sarcomeres were significantly shorter in dmd larvae (n = 356 sarcomeres dmd control [four fish total], n = 282 sarcomeres WT sibling [three fish total]; p<0.0001; one biological replicate), with a mean length of 1.575 ± 0.1567 µm (Figure 7B2, B4).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy measurements shown in Figure 7B2 and B4.

claim: The finding of shorter sarcomeres in dmd larvae corresponds with previous studies.
source: This result corresponded with previous studies that showed shorter sarcomeres in dmd larvae (Widrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Widrick et al., 2016.

claim: Three sessions of eNMES significantly increased mean sarcomere lengths (1.707 ± 0.1710 µm) compared to dmd mutant controls.
source: Three sessions of eNMES significantly increased mean sarcomere lengths (1.707 ± 0.1710 µm) compared to dmd mutant controls (n = 356 sarcomeres dmd control [four fish total], n = 550 sarcomeres eNMES [four fish total]; p<0.0001; one biological replicate) (Figure 7B3, B4).
evidence: This claim is supported by SHG microscopy measurements shown in Figure 7B3 and B4.

claim: eNMES-treated dmd larvae still had shorter sarcomeres than WT siblings.
source: Although eNMES-treated dmd larvae still had shorter sarcomeres than WT siblings, these data suggest the hypothesis that eNMES may improve muscle structure and function by restoring sarcomere lengths to more optimal lengths.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sarcomere length measurements.

claim: eNMES may improve muscle structure and function by restoring sarcomere lengths to more optimal lengths.
source: Although eNMES-treated dmd larvae still had shorter sarcomeres than WT siblings, these data suggest the hypothesis that eNMES may improve muscle structure and function by restoring sarcomere lengths to more optimal lengths.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the sarcomere length data.

claim: Myonuclear size and shape play an important role in muscle health.
source: Myonuclear size and shape play an important role in muscle health (Folker and Baylies, 2013; Roman and Gomes, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Folker and Baylies, 2013 and Roman and Gomes, 2018.

claim: A higher filament index indicates that nuclei are more elongated, which is suggested to be healthier.
source: A circle has a filament index of 1, and a higher filament index indicates a departure to a more ellipsoidal shape. Thus, a higher filament index indicates that nuclei are more elongated, which is suggested to be healthier (Bruusgaard et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bruusgaard et al., 2003.

claim: Muscle nuclei in dmd mutants had significantly lower volumes compared to WT siblings.
